transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I'm a construction manager, have been for about twenty years now. Started out framing houses back in the day with my brother-in-law, actually. He's retired now, bought a place down in Florida. Keeps telling me I need to come down and go deep-sea fishing with him, but honestly, I don't know if I could handle being out on a boat that long. My stomach's never been great with the rocking. 

But anyway, I'm here because... well, it's getting really bad at work. Every time I have to get near a scaffold, or a roof edge, or even just an upper platform, my head just starts screaming at me that I'm going to go over. Even when I'm looking right at the safety rails, and I checked the setup myself, I know it's safe... but it's like my brain doesn't believe it. It's ridiculous, I know. I used to be able to walk beams like it was nothing. My old boss, Frank, he used to say I was part mountain goat. Frank was a character, he actually drove this old beat-up El Camino to the sites...
Do you experience these fears or feelings of impending danger when you're not at work?

Well, you know, it's funny you ask that, because I was just talking to my wife about this the other day. We were at the mall—she loves that new outlet center they built off I-95, the one with the huge food court. They have this pretzel place there, unbelievable. Best pretzels I've ever had. We usually grab one and sit by the fountain. But anyway, to answer your question... no, not really. It's just the heights. Like, I don't feel that panic if I'm just walking around the neighborhood or driving. Speaking of driving, they've been doing all that roadwork on my commute, tearing up the asphalt for weeks. It's a nightmare. I swear, the guys running the pavers don't know what they're doing half the time. But yeah, no, it's just when I'm up high. If I'm on solid ground, I'm fine.
Does this fear of heights happen when you're not working, but still in a high place, like hiking or looking out from a high floor in a building?

Yeah, it definitely does. It's not just a work thing. We went to the city a few months back to see my daughter—she just started at NYU, actually. Doing pre-law, which I don't know where she gets the brains for that, neither me nor my wife are big readers. But she's loving it, she's got this tiny little dorm room that costs more than my first mortgage. Anyway, we went to this restaurant she wanted to try, one of those places on the top floor of a skyscraper, you know? Supposed to have these amazing views. And I couldn't even go near the window. I spent the whole dinner staring at my plate, sweating, gripping the edge of the table. My wife had to order for me because I couldn't even focus on the menu. The steak was good, though, I think it was a ribeye. But yeah, hiking too. We used to go up to the Adirondacks every fall, rent a cabin near Lake George. Beautiful up there, the leaves turning all those colors. But the last time we tried to hike up one of the trails that gets near a cliff edge, I just froze. Couldn't move. Had to turn back. Ruined the whole afternoon for everyone. My wife was understanding, but you know, she loves hiking. She's got all the gear, the boots, the walking sticks... I just feel terrible holding her back like that.
Has your fear of heights started to affect your social life or leisure activities beyond just hiking and visiting high places?

Well, as far as social stuff, I mean, I guess I've been making excuses to avoid going to my buddy Dave's apartment because he's on the 15th floor with a balcony. Dave's a great guy, we used to bowl in a league together. Our team was called the Pin Pals, which, you know, is a terrible pun, but Dave thought it was hilarious. He's got this bowling ball that looks like a giant eyeball, creeps me out a little bit, honestly. 

But really, where it's hitting me hardest is work. It's getting bad. I’ve missed or delayed so many upper-level walk-throughs lately. The crews and the subcontractors, they're starting to look at me funny, questioning my calls on things because they know I haven't been up there to look at it myself. Which, you know, you can't manage a site from the ground. You just can't. You miss things. Like this one time, a sub tried to use interior-grade screws on an exterior deck frame. If I hadn't caught that... man. But now, it's gotten to the point where the company's insurer actually pushed for an occupational health review. They noticed I wasn't completing key safety inspections on the upper floors. And you don't want to mess with the insurance guys. They wear these cheap suits and carry clipboards, but they hold all the cards, you know? So yeah, it's... it's definitely affecting things.
Are you finding it difficult to perform daily tasks or chores at home because of your fear of heights?

At home? No, not really. We live in a single-story ranch, actually. Best decision we ever made, buying that place. We picked it up back in '08 when the market completely tanked, got an absolute steal on it. It’s got this big backyard, which is great because my wife loves to garden. She's got these raised beds she built herself—well, I helped her level them out, but she did all the planting. Tomatoes, zucchini, peppers, you name it. The zucchini gets totally out of control by August, we end up giving it away in grocery bags to the neighbors whether they want it or not. 

But as far as chores go... no, I don't really have to deal with heights at the house. I guess cleaning the gutters would be one, but I just hire a neighborhood kid to do that now. There's this massive oak tree out front that just dumps leaves everywhere. It's a beautiful tree, must be fifty years old, provides great shade in the summer, but man, the mess it makes in the fall is unbelievable. So yeah, I just pay a guy a few bucks to clear the roof and the gutters. Other than that, around the house I'm totally fine. I just keep my feet on the floor and do the ground-level stuff.
Has your fear of heights caused any problems in your relationships with family or friends?

No, not really. I mean, my wife has been great about it, like I said with the hiking. She's really patient. We've been married almost twenty years now, which is crazy to think about. We met at this terrible dive bar downtown, place is a bank now, of course. Everything turns into a bank or a pharmacy eventually, doesn't it? But yeah, we met there, and I spilled half a pitcher of cheap beer on her shoes. I thought she was gonna kill me, but she just laughed. She's got a great laugh. 

But no, nobody's really giving me a hard time about the heights thing, aside from the guys at work, maybe. Dave doesn't care if I don't come over to his place, we just meet up at the bowling alley or grab a burger at this diner we like. They make a fantastic patty melt, by the way. On rye, with those caramelized onions. I try not to eat too much red meat anymore, my cholesterol was creeping up a bit last time I saw my regular doctor, but sometimes you just gotta have a patty melt, you know? So yeah, family and friends, we're all good. No real issues there.
Are you feeling anxious or uneasy even when you're not in a situation involving heights?

No, not really. If I'm on the ground, I'm fine. I don't just sit around worrying about it, you know? Like, when I'm driving to work, I'm not thinking about heights. I'm usually listening to sports radio. I love listening to the morning show guys argue about the local baseball team. They've got this one host, Mike, who just loses his mind every time the manager makes a pitching change. It's hilarious. Honestly, I think the manager is doing the best he can with the bullpen he's got. You can't expect a guy to throw strikes when his arm is hanging by a thread, right? They really need to trade for a solid lefty reliever before the deadline. But yeah, no, I feel totally normal when I'm just going about my day, as long as I don't have to go up anywhere.
When did you first notice your fear of heights?

Well, it all started about thirteen months ago. Yeah, just over a year. There was this accident at work with a stair tower... but honestly, that whole site was a mess from day one. We had this subcontractor doing the concrete work, and they were always behind schedule. Always. I'd be on the phone with the guy, Tony, I think his name was, and he'd give me these excuses about the supply chain or the weather. Like, come on, Tony, it rained for two hours on a Tuesday, that doesn't put you three weeks behind. It drove me crazy. I'm the one who has to answer to the client, you know? And the client on that job was this developer who wanted everything done yesterday but didn't want to pay for overtime. He drove this ridiculous sports car to the dirt lot, always complaining about the dust. Like, buddy, it's a construction site, what do you expect? But yeah, the stair tower thing... that's when this whole heights issue really started for me.
Are there any other activities or situations in your daily life, beyond work and heights, where you feel like your fear or anxiety is holding you back?

No, not really. Aside from the heights, I'm good. I mean, I still go to the grocery store, I still take the dog for a walk. We have this golden retriever, Buster, he's basically a giant toddler. He refuses to walk past this one specific fire hydrant down the street without sniffing it for at least three minutes. I've timed it. Three minutes. And if I try to pull him away, he just drops all his weight and turns into a furry boulder. It's ridiculous. But you know, my wife wanted a dog, and you know what they say, happy wife, happy life. We actually got him from this rescue out in the county, run by this older couple who must have had twenty dogs running around their farm. They were making homemade dog treats when we went to pick him up, smelled like peanut butter and bacon. Smelled better than half the things I cook, honestly. I tried getting into smoking meats last summer—got a whole setup, the wood chips, the thermometer—but I ended up drying out a brisket so bad you could have used it as a doorstop. So I stick to grilling burgers now. But yeah, to answer your question, no, nothing else is really holding me back. Just the heights.
Have you been avoiding certain activities or places because of your fear of heights?

Yeah, definitely. I mean, I've been doing everything I can to get out of it. I've been handing off all the height inspections to my foremen. I just tell them I'm tied up with paperwork or something. And if we have a site meeting that's supposed to be on an upper floor, I make them move it down to the ground level. I just say it's easier for everyone to access, which, you know, makes sense anyway. 

But sometimes I absolutely have to go up, like if the client is there and insists on seeing the progress on the fourth floor. When that happens, I make sure one of my guys is right beside me the whole time. I basically glue myself to them and just rush through it as fast as humanly possible, just sweating and terrified the entire time. 

It's embarrassing, honestly. Especially in front of the guys. Construction guys aren't exactly known for being sensitive, you know? Like this one guy, Smitty, he runs the framing crew. The guy's been doing this for thirty years and he's got forearms like Popeye. He eats nails for breakfast, I swear. He showed up to work last winter in a t-shirt when it was twenty degrees out. I asked him if he was cold and he just grunted and drank his black coffee. I don't even think he feels pain. He smashed his thumb with a hammer once and didn't even blink, just wrapped it in electrical tape and kept going. That tape is like duct tape for electricians, they use it for everything. But yeah, having to act like a scared kid in front of guys like Smitty... it's not a good look for a manager.
